design_detail: Exchange of letters in Science (6 June 2003, vol. 300, pp. 1504-1505): a letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin criticizing the 2002 report of severe dopaminergic neurotoxicity in primates given MDMA (Ricaurte et al., 2002), followed on the same pages by the reply of Ricaurte, Yuan, Hatzidimitriou, Cord and McCann. The letter is one paragraph with 16 references; the reply has five paragraphs and 15 references. No data. The PDF also carries unrelated letters on p. 1503 (smallpox modelling) and p. 1505 (research fraud and gun control), which are not part of this card. The exchange predates the 2003 retraction of the primate study; the 2002 paper and its retraction notice are not in this batch and are described here only as these letters and Barnett and Doblin (2021) describe them.
can_establish: What critics and the authors of the 2002 primate study argued about it in June 2003, before its retraction, and which human studies each side cited.
cannot_establish: Whether MDMA damages dopamine or serotonin neurons in people: neither letter presents data, and the study under discussion was later retracted (as Barnett and Doblin, 2021, report).

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (letters). The study discussed gave MDMA, as then believed, to ten monkeys (reply, 1st paragraph).
sample.selection_effects: Each side cites the studies that support its position; the reply relies largely on its authors' own work (refs 9-13 of the reply).

exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not reported here as numbers. The two sides disagree on whether the regimen in the primate study modelled common human use; the reply argues that the dosing pattern, not only the amount, determined which neurotransmitter systems were affected in the animals.
exposure.polysubstance: Not discussed for the human studies cited.

outcomes.instruments: Cited human measures: brain dopamine transporter imaging (letter refs 7-8), a post-mortem case (ref 9), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) dopamine metabolites (refs 10-12), serotonin transporter and memory in clinical studies (refs 3, 15, 16).
outcomes.validity_norms: The reply argues that CSF homovanillic acid (HVA) is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity (reply, 3rd paragraph, refs 11-12).

analysis.effect_sizes: None given, except the reply's counts of US emergency-room visits related to MDMA (500 in 1994, about 4500 in 2000) and its statement that one of ten monkeys died.
analysis.selective_reporting: The letter describes the earlier CSF studies by the same research group as finding no reduced dopamine metabolites; one of the three it cites (McCann et al., 1994) reports lower CSF HVA in its MDMA group (see reporting issues). The reply does not correct this.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Two opposed readings of a primate study, each supported by selected citations: the critics cite imaging and post-mortem reports of normal dopamine markers and earlier CSF findings in people who used MDMA heavily; the authors cite mouse studies, their own primate observation that the pattern of dosing changed the toxic profile, and dopamine-transporter reductions in people who had used methamphetamine.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The letter states that there is no credible evidence linking amphetamine-type prescription drugs to Parkinson's disease and that clinical MDMA research has been conducted without evidence of toxicity; its support for the first is a news-service item (ref 14), and the reply states that none of the three studies cited for the second measured neurotoxicity. The reply concludes that the data are insufficient to say clinical MDMA research carries no risk of monoaminergic injury. In September 2003 the primate paper was retracted because, as its authors then reported, all but one animal had received methamphetamine rather than MDMA (Barnett and Doblin, 2021, p. 2 of the online-first PDF): the reply's argument from the primate data, written before that discovery, therefore concerned animals that had mostly been given another drug.

timeline.event: Ricaurte et al. (2002) report severe dopaminergic and less severe serotonergic neurotoxicity in ten primates given what the title calls a common recreational dose regimen of MDMA (as described by Barnett and Doblin, 2021, and in this exchange).
This exchange (6 June 2003), before the retraction.
Retraction in Science (September 2003): methamphetamine rather than MDMA had been given to all but one animal because of a labelling error, as reported by Barnett and Doblin (2021).
Study of US newspaper coverage of the publication and of the retraction.

replication.where_it_stands: The primate dopamine finding that both letters argue about was withdrawn with the retraction. The human points raised in the exchange (dopamine markers in people who used MDMA heavily, the sensitivity of CSF HVA) remain to be judged from the primary studies, which are not cards in this batch except McCann et al. (1994).

funding.declared_conflicts: No statements of interests are printed for either letter.
funding.affiliations_note: Letter: Michael Mithoefer (Mount Pleasant, South Carolina), Lisa Jerome and Richard Doblin (Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies, MAPS; the corresponding address is a MAPS e-mail). Barnett and Doblin (2021, p. 5 of the online-first PDF) describe Doblin as the founder and executive director of MAPS, which funds research on the therapeutic potential of MDMA. Reply: the authors of the criticized study (Johns Hopkins University School of Medicine). Both sides had a stake in the outcome; recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount either.

what_would_settle_it: For the human question the letters raise: dopamine transporter imaging and CSF metabolite measures in people with heavy MDMA use and little stimulant use, against matched controls and with repeat measures over abstinence; for the animal question: replication in primates with the identity of the drug verified.

domains.note: Letters; citations chosen by each side.
The letter misdescribes one of its own CSF sources and relies on a news item; the reply does not appraise the studies it cites.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: The reply rests mainly on its authors' own studies, including the one under criticism.
Both sides go beyond their citations: absence of risk on one side, parkinsonism-like features on the other.

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for and against dopamine neurotoxicity of MDMA in people
domains.note: Each letter is one-sided, but together the exchange presents both positions.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to letters (METHODS §5.3); the editors' narrative-review checklist is used for the exchange as a whole. It may be cited for what each side argued before the retraction; it is not evidence on whether MDMA damages dopamine or serotonin neurons.

key_findings.finding: The letter argues that because people rarely die from MDMA use, the high mortality among the primates suggests the study did not model a common recreational regimen, which calls its interspecies scaling into question; it also says the paper's position conflicts with an earlier monkey study by the same group (ref 6).
key_findings.locator: Letter by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin (left column, one paragraph)

key_findings.finding: The letter says the paper raises the possibility that even one night's recreational use may cause dopamine toxicity and a higher risk of Parkinson's disease, but does not cite studies finding normal dopamine (with reduced serotonin) in people who used MDMA heavily: two imaging studies of the dopamine transporter (refs 7-8) and a post-mortem examination of one person (ref 9); and that earlier studies by Ricaurte and McCann in people who used MDMA heavily did not find reduced dopamine metabolites in CSF (refs 10-12).
key_findings.locator: Letter (left column), middle of the paragraph
key_findings.note: Contradicted for ref 11 by that study's own table; see reporting issue 0.

key_findings.finding: The letter states that the dopamine changes reported are long-known potential effects of d-amphetamine and d-methamphetamine, available on prescription for over 80 years; that there is no credible evidence linking these drugs to Parkinson's disease or to more early-onset Parkinson's disease (ref 14, a New Scientist news item); and that clinical MDMA research has been conducted without evidence of toxicity, including no detectable change in serotonin transporter or memory (refs 3, 15, 16).
key_findings.locator: Letter (left column), end of the paragraph

key_findings.finding: Reply: interspecies dose scaling was not used in the recent studies; one of ten monkeys given the regimen died of complications related to hyperthermia, from which the authors say no firm conclusion about mortality can be drawn given the sample size; isolated human deaths with prominent hyperthermia have been described (refs 2-5); and US emergency-room visits related to MDMA rose from 500 in 1994 to about 4500 in 2000, a significant portion involving raised body temperature.

Reply: the letter ignores mouse studies showing MDMA dopamine neurotoxicity (ref 10) and the study's central observation that changing the pattern of dosing changed the toxic profile in primates (from serotonin alone to dopamine and serotonin); because the human studies cited did not take patterns of use into account, their groups were probably heterogeneous and dopamine markers, including the transporter, would not be expected to differ; and CSF HVA is neither a sensitive nor a specific marker of dopamine neurotoxicity (refs 11-12).

Reply: methamphetamine and d-amphetamine are dopamine neurotoxins with no evidence that they cause parkinsonism, but past methamphetamine use has been associated with lower dopamine transporter levels in living, abstinent people (refs 13-15) and with motor slowing (ref 15), features seen in parkinsonism.
key_findings.locator: Response, 4th paragraph (p. 1504 right column, continued on p. 1505)

key_findings.finding: Reply: of the three references the letter gives for clinical research without toxicity, one is an unpublished conference presentation, one is an exchange of letters about interspecies dose scaling, and one is a Phase I study of two doses and placebo in which no neurotoxicity measures were taken; the authors remain of the opinion that the data do not show that clinical MDMA research can be done without risk of monoaminergic neural injury.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter says earlier studies by Ricaurte and McCann found no reduced dopamine metabolites in CSF (refs 10-12). Ref 11 is McCann et al. (1994), whose Table 4 shows CSF HVA of 19.4 (SD 7.8) ng/ml in 30 people who used MDMA against 27.4 (SD 21.3) in 28 controls, with a significant group effect (F[1,52]=6.9, p=.01) and a group-by-sex interaction: lower in women who used MDMA, not different in men (checked by this reader in the McCann et al. 1994 PDF, pp. 132-133; the abstract of that paper mentions only 5-HIAA). The reply accepts the letter's description and argues instead that CSF HVA is an insensitive marker.
reporting_issues.consequence: The letter's argument from normal CSF dopamine metabolites is not accurate for at least one of its sources; the lower HVA in that study is itself a finding the CSF claims for this monograph should report.

reporting_issues.issue: Mortality in the primate study is described differently in the sources read: the letter speaks of high mortality, the reply says one of ten monkeys died, and Barnett and Doblin (2021, p. 2 of the online-first PDF) say two of the animals died. The 2002 paper itself was not read.
reporting_issues.consequence: Any statement about deaths in the primate study must name its source and should be checked against the paper or its retraction notice.

reporting_issues.issue: The letter's support for the absence of any Parkinson's link is a news-service item (ref 14), and the reply states that none of the three sources cited for the absence of toxicity in clinical research measured neurotoxicity; the letter's reference list shows one of them to be a conference paper (ref 16).
reporting_issues.consequence: The letter's two strongest reassurances rest on sources that cannot carry them.

reporting_issues.issue: Crossref lists G. A. Ricaurte among the authors of this item because the letter and the reply share a DOI and pages; the letter is signed by Mithoefer, Jerome and Doblin and the reply by Ricaurte and four colleagues (already noted on the reference record).
reporting_issues.consequence: Cite the reply as part of the same item, naming its authors in the text.

verification.source_read: PDF pp. 1503-1505 (PDFs/MDMA/Mithoefer_2003_ScienceCorrespondence.pdf): the letter (p. 1504) and the reply (pp. 1504-1505) read in full and p. 1504 rendered; the unrelated letters on pp. 1503 and 1505 were not used. The CSF statement was checked against McCann et al. (1994), PDF pp. 129 and 132-133.
